GEORGIA SUMMARY SGP RESULTS
CORRELATIONS BETWEEN GROWTH AND PRIOR ACHIEVEMENT

 Damian W Betebenner & Adam VanIwaarden
 National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment
 Dover, New Hampshire September 15th, 2016

ISSUE: BACKGROUND

• Initial SGP analyses with preliminary 2016 ELA and Mathematics EOG
 data were completed in late July. Preliminary EOC data was also available

• As part of validation of results, correlations between mean prior
 achievement (mean of prior scale score standardized within grade) and
 mean SGP (unadjusted and SIMEX adjusted) were examined at the school
 level.

• In all but one content area, the correlations increased from 2015 to 2016.

• We want to explore whether these increases reflect a change in the
 system or are a manifestation of the model (e.g., measurement error).

ASSESSMENT: BACKGROUND

• 2015 was the first year for the Georgia Milestones (CRCT/EOCT
 independent variables/Milestones dependent variable)

• 2016 was the second year for the Georgia Milestones (CRCT &
 Milestones independent variables/Milestones dependent variable)

ASSESSMENT: BACKGROUND
• In an attempt to isolate the cause of the increases in correlation, we examined
 Mathematics, Social Studies and Science.

 • In 2015, ELA analyses used Reading & ELA from 2014 and earlier CRCT as priors
 (two-priors/year). In 2016, ELA analyses used one 2015 ELA prior and multiple
 2014 priors (CRCT reading and ELA).

 • The new Milestones ELA test incorporates reading, language arts, and writing.

 • Result for 2016 EOG tests (ELA, Mathematics, Science, and Social Studies) have
 been finalized. EOC test results are not finalized yet (it is unexpected that the
 results will change significantly).

• The best “apples-to-apples” comparisons emerged from the EOG tests with
 consistent priors (Mathematics, Social Studies, Science)

ANALYSIS: RESULTS
• From 2015 to 2016 there is a definite trend upward in correlations
 between prior achievement and growth.

• Examination of data (see supplementary scatterplots) rule out outliers/
 changes in marginal distributions as the reason.

 • For example, non-random assignment of students to school by level of
 achievement is one of the factors for measurement error bias. Yet no
 marked changes in stratification of schools based upon achievement
 was observed.

• The increasing correlations observed are synonymous with larger
 increases in mean SGP for schools serving higher achieving students
 (higher mean achievement) than their counterparts serving lower
 achieving students.

 supplementary scatterplots)

ANALYSIS: RESULTS
• To investigate more broadly, we examined results associated with
 assessment transitions in 7 states:

 • 2 non-consortium affiliated states (including Georgia)

 • 2 PARCC affiliated states

 • 3 SBAC affiliated states

• All summary statistics calculated using a 15 student minimum.

ANALYSIS: CONCLUSIONS

• Results suggest that increasing correlations are not associated with
 model anomalies but reflect actual changes occurring with Georgia
 schools.

• The results suggest that in the second year of Georgia Milestones
 anchored to new achievement standards, schools serving higher
 achieving students are transitioning better than schools serving lower
 achieving students.

• We welcome any advice on how we might continue to investigate
 this phenomenon to reach definitive conclusions.
